message.content:
**CPU (Central Processing Unit)**  
* **Purpose:** General‑purpose processor designed to handle a wide variety of tasks. It excels at executing complex instructions one or few threads at a time.  
* **Architecture:** Few cores (typically 2–32) but each core is powerful, featuring deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, and large caches.  
* **Use cases:** Operating systems, application logic, database queries, web servers, gaming engines’ main loop, etc., where latency matters more than raw throughput.  

---

**GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)**  
* **Purpose:** Specialized hardware originally built for rendering graphics—massively parallel processing of many similar operations on huge data sets. Modern GPUs have evolved into highly programmable units used for scientific computing, machine learning, video encoding/decoding, cryptocurrency mining, etc.  
* **Architecture:** Hundreds to thousands of lightweight cores arranged in SIMD/SIMT groups. Each core handles simple arithmetic quickly, but they’re not optimized for branching or cache‑intensive workloads. They rely heavily on high memory bandwidth rather than low latency.  
* **Use cases:** Rendering frames, training neural networks, performing matrix multiplications, running physics simulations, real‑time ray tracing, etc.—tasks that can be broken down into many identical small computations performed simultaneously.  

---

### Key Differences Summarized

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Core count | Low (≤ 64) | Very High (> 2000) |
| Core complexity | High – full instruction set, caching, speculative exec | Simple – fixed pipeline, minimal control flow |
| Workload type | Serial / irregular, heavy branching | Parallel, regular, compute‑heavy |
| Latency vs Throughput | Optimized for low latency per thread | Optimized for high throughput across many threads |
| Memory hierarchy | Large L1/L2/L3 caches, lower bandwidth | Huge shared memory & registers, very high bandwidth |
| Typical use | OS kernels, applications, databases | Graphics rendering, ML inference/training, HPC |

In short, CPUs are “generalists” good at handling diverse, sequential work efficiently, while GPUs are “specialists” engineered to perform the same operation over massive amounts of data concurrently.
